channel.title: Paper Pulse
channel.description: Keyword-based research paper aggregation from arXiv and IACR

item.title: Enforcing Winner-Only Disclosure: Verifiable Tally Hiding for Weighted DAO Governance
item.description:
## Core Contribution This paper presents a **verifiable winner-only tally-hiding construction** for weighted binary voting in DAO governance. Registered weights are bound to credentials via zero-knowledge ballots, while weighted contributions remain encrypted through aggregation and threshold comparison, ensuring the only plaintext output is the final outcome bit.
## Method & Verification The system combines blockchain-based ballot adjudication with an off-chain encrypted computation backend. Exact ciphertext and transcript bindings allow any public verifier to confirm that the published outcome corresponds to accepted ballots.
## Key Results For a bounded 8-voter, 8-bit instance (134 encrypted gates, 3-of-5 trustee release), we formally prove **passive-observer backend transcript privacy** under honest execution by all five trustees. Privacy against malicious sub-threshold trustees remains an open challenge.

item.title: Multi-PGBF: Efficient Oblivious Key-Value Store and Application to Private Set Intersection
item.description:
**Core Contribution**: We propose Multi-PGBF, an efficient oblivious key-value store (OKVS) that recursively combines multiple Peelable Garbled Bloom Filters (PGBF) to eliminate the non-empty core issue at low expansion rates, plus a clustered variant C-Multi-PGBF for faster encoding.
**Key Results**: Experiments show Multi-PGBF improves encoding time by 65.1%–77.6% over RR (CCS’22), and C-Multi-PGBF by 60.2%–64.7% over the clustered RR variant. For decoding, Multi-PGBF is 28.6%–62.4% faster than RR and 89.7%–96.3% faster than RB-OKVS (Usenix’23). When integrated into state-of-the-art two-party and multi-party private set intersection protocols (Eurocrypt’21, Usenix’24), our constructions yield faster protocols in most settings.
**Impact**: This work provides a high-performance OKVS building block, advancing privacy-preserving applications requiring large-scale data processing.

item.title: New Lower Bounds for Rows of $d$-Disjunct Matrices via Recursive Potentials
item.description:
## Core Contribution This paper improves the lower bound for the minimum number of rows $T(d)$ in $d$-disjunct matrices used in nonadaptive combinatorial group testing.
## Key Result We prove $T(d)\ge 0.9283d^2 - O(d)$, significantly strengthening the previous best bound of $\frac{15+\sqrt{33}}{24}d^2 \approx 0.8643d^2$ by Shangguan and Ge (2016).
## Method Our approach introduces a **column-deletion recurrence** where the light-heavy threshold varies dynamically with the recursive state $z=(n-t)/d^2$, instead of remaining fixed. The analytic core reduces to a first-order ODE, and a self-contained **interval-arithmetic certificate** rigorously verifies that the solution reaches the required contact point, providing a machine-checkable proof.
## Significance This work demonstrates the power of combining recursive potential functions with computer-assisted verification, yielding a substantial constant-factor improvement and narrowing the gap to known upper bounds.

item.title: How Many Traces Suffice? PAC Guarantees for Profiled and Non-profiled Side-Channel Analysis
item.description:
## Core Contribution This paper introduces a **Probably Approximately Correct (PAC)** framework for profiled and non-profiled side-channel analysis (SCA), transforming trace complexity from an empirical metric into a reusable finite-sample criterion for key recovery.
## Key Innovation The framework separates **finite-sample estimation error** from the **intrinsic separability** between the correct key and competing hypotheses. This distinction enables confidence guarantees on key rank and diagnoses whether attack failures stem from insufficient data or inherently weak score discrimination.
## Main Results Experiments on ASCAD-f and ASCAD-r demonstrate practical competitiveness: the profiled attack achieves exact recovery with tens of attack traces, while the non-profiled rank certificate guarantees recovery with ~1,000 traces—substantially below prior reported minima. The framework is also generalizable to other learners/distinguishers via corresponding score-gap guarantees.
## Significance This work provides the first PAC-style theoretical grounding for trace complexity in SCA, offering both confidence bounds and practical performance competitive with state-of-the-art attacks.

item.title: Rank Measures and Exponential Lower Bounds for Multilinear Secret Sharing
item.description:
## Core Contribution This paper proves that the **Razborov–Gál rank measure survives amortization** in multilinear secret sharing: the normalized size of any multi-target monotone span program is at least the rank measure of the function it computes.
## Key Results - Combined with Pitassi–Robere's rank witnesses, we obtain an **explicit family of access structures** where every perfect multilinear scheme over any finite field has average and maximum information ratio $2^{\Omega(n)}$. - This settles Beimel's open question, showing the worst-case multilinear information ratio is $2^{\Theta(n)}$—an exponential improvement over the previous quasipolynomial bound. - The bound extends to schemes with arbitrary sharing algorithms and affine-linear reconstruction, under pairwise statistical privacy below one, yielding exponential normalized lower bounds for every fixed reconstruction degree when the secret dimension is $2^{o(n)}$.
## Significance This is the **first exponential lower bound** for general multilinear secret sharing, demonstrating that amortization does not weaken rank-based arguments. The unified framework covers both perfect and statistical privacy, broadening the applicability of rank measures in cryptographic complexity.

item.title: Constant-round MPC protocols with Fall-back Security
item.description:
## Core Contributions This paper investigates the **round complexity** of MPC with fall-back security under threshold corruption, achieving **constant-round protocols** for optimal thresholds.
## Key Results 1. **Semi-honest setting**: A **3-round** fall-back secure protocol for \( t < n/2 \) in the plain model, improving the prior best of 11 rounds by nearly 4×.
2. **Malicious setting**: A **4-round** protocol in the CRS model satisfying unanimous abort (UA) — the **first constant-round** maliciously fall-back secure protocol.
3. **Fairness extension**: A **5-round** protocol achieving fairness against unbounded adversaries for \( t < n/2 \) corruptions, while maintaining UA against PPT adversaries for any larger corruption set.
## Significance This work breaks the previous linear-round barrier, demonstrating that fall-back security is achievable in constant rounds. All protocols attain optimal corruption thresholds, providing both theoretical advances and practical efficiency improvements for secure computation in dynamic adversarial environments.

item.title: Circle-Linear Cryptanalysis: Bibrace Characters and Weak-Key Linear Distinguishers for CRAFT
item.description:
## Abstract This paper introduces **circle-linear cryptanalysis**, a novel framework that extends linear cryptanalysis to arbitrary finite abelian groups defined by a **binary bibrace** structure. Only half of the traditional linear masks remain valid; the rest become quadratic. Instantiating the framework on a specific bibrace group, the authors analyze the lightweight cipher **CRAFT**.
The Midori/CRAFT S-box exhibits four probability-one linear relations forming a small subgroup preserved in both directions. Within this subgroup, mask propagation is deterministic and linear, reducing the best-trail search to a minimum-weight codeword problem solved exactly via complete enumeration.
A key innovation is the **joint analysis of key addition and diffusion**, yielding weak-key classes several bits larger than naive cell-by-cell analysis. Notably, CRAFT's round constants impose no additional restrictions. The authors construct weak-key distinguishers up to **18 rounds**; at 14 rounds, the squared correlation is 2⁻⁴⁴ over 2¹⁰⁸ keys, versus 2⁻⁶²·¹² for the designers' linear hull (valid for all keys). This improves the best linear correlation by 18 bits at equal rounds and extends four rounds further. All results are experimentally verified with random-key negative controls.

item.title: Eavesdropper-Blind Remote State Preparation and Applications to Quantum Public-Key Encryption
item.description: ## Core Contributions This paper introduces **eavesdropper-blind remote state preparation (EB-RSP)**, a relaxed RSP notion requiring blindness only against external observers, not the quantum server. Despite the weaker adversarial model, we prove that **two-message EB-RSP suffices for quantum public-key encryption** with classical keys and quantum ciphertexts. We construct two-message EB-RSP from **one-way group actions** (avoiding trapdoor assumptions), and show existing TCF-based RSP protocols can be naturally adapted to this notion. This work provides the first trapdoor-free RSP-type primitive and demonstrates that meaningful cryptographic applications remain achievable under significantly weaker security requirements.

item.title: Exact linear correlations and the cost of Walsh-transform key recovery, with application to SPEEDY
item.description:
## Core Contribution This paper establishes an exact linear cryptanalysis framework for cipher rounds where two S-box layers are separated by no key addition, showing that the round correlation is a signed sum over intermediate masks—not a product of layer correlations. We develop four key tools: an exact one-round algorithm with a decidable product-rule condition, dependency-graph decomposition, a covering-number bound that strengthens linear-trail weight limits, and a Walsh-support criterion linking affine dimension to key-recovery cost.
## Key Results for SPEEDY Applying this framework revises published cryptanalysis of SPEEDY: a reported five-round mask sequence has exact correlation $2^{-90.0962}$ (not $2^{-93.0147}$); the unrestricted five-round weight bound rises from 53.7714 to 62.2616 bits; the claimed full-round attack on SPEEDY-7-192 at $2^{158.06}$ actually requires at least $2^{199.97}$ encryptions. For SPEEDY-6-192, we provide a six-round attack (data $2^{169.84}$, time $2^{170.20}$, memory $2^{156}$) and prove no attack in this class has both data and time below $2^{128}$, with a time lower bound of $2^{136.302}$. A four-round differential-linear correlation is also corrected.
## Significance Our work demonstrates that exact intra-round correlation evaluation can fundamentally alter security assessments, providing both a rigorous theoretical framework and tighter bounds for SPEEDY.

item.title: Two Novel Multidimensional Affine Variations of the Hill Cipher
item.description: ## Summary This paper presents two novel symmetric multidimensional affine nested variants of the Hill Cipher, a block polygraphic substitution scheme based on linear transformation of plaintext into ciphertext. The first variant employs invertible key matrices of orders 2, 4, and 8, where the 2×2 matrix values rotate with each character block (akin to the rotating wheels of a German Enigma machine), with outputs cascading through 4×4 and 8×8 matrices, then back through 4×4 and rotating 2×2 matrices. The second variant uses orders 4, 8, and 16 without rotation. Both variants apply XOR vectors to plaintext blocks before matrix multiplication to create affine ciphers. The discussion covers strengths, weaknesses, and proposes a more robust character set with increased modulus, alongside analysis of affine XOR vector trade-offs.

item.title: Multidimensional Hill Cipher Substitution– Permutation Network
item.description: ## Key Contribution **MD-Hill-SPN** is the first Hill-cipher construction integrating a multi-tier diffusion layer, a memory-hard KDF, and simultaneous multi-metric empirical validation. Two independent full-suite runs confirm: (a) full plaintext avalanche from round 1 (mean 63.97–64.67 of 128 bits vs. ideal 64); (b) differential-probability sampling floor of 2×10⁻⁵ reached at round 4 (50,000/50,000 distinct output differences); (c) algebraic-degree lower-bound saturation from round 1; (d) linear bias indistinguishable from random (4.40% exceedance, below 4.55% noise floor); and (e) Singleton-bound (MDS) branch numbers for all tiers (B=5/9/17 for 4×4/8×8/16×16), exhaustively computed over weight-1 inputs. This work moves Hill ciphers beyond theoretical design to an empirically validated framework under single-key, known-plaintext, fixed-parameter conditions—a comprehensive evaluation no prior Hill variant has reported.

item.title: Pilaf: Fully Tight Two-Round Threshold Signatures with Adaptive Corruptions
item.description: We present $\mathsf{TPilaf}$, the first two-round threshold signature scheme achieving fully tight security against adaptive corruptions while supporting partially non-interactive signing. The scheme is pairing-free, built on prime-order groups under the $\mathsf{MDDH}$ assumption in the random-oracle model, with offline-preprocessable first-round messages and aggregatable second-round shares. Our proof introduces two novel tools: a linearly homomorphic dual-mode commitment with targetable opening (enabling the simulator to open fixed commitments to later Fiat-Shamir challenges), and profile-wise zero-sum masking with posterior completion (ensuring corruption openings and signing responses follow exact conditional laws). These enable a delayed branch-decision reduction that eliminates all combinatorial losses in user count, threshold, sessions, or corruption patterns, yielding a bound containing only explicit bad-event and assumption terms.

item.title: Lightweight Lattice-based Single-Party Public-Key Authenticated Key Exchange
item.description: This paper addresses the challenge of designing lightweight, post-quantum Authenticated Key Exchange (AKE) for resource-constrained IoT environments. We revisit the ALIKE framework (ISO/IEC 29192-4) and bridge its gap in the quantum era through three contributions: (1) we prove that the Hash-Before-Encrypt (HBE) paradigm generically transforms deterministic OW-CPA schemes into OW-CCA-secure ones; (2) we modify Bai et al.'s efficient lattice-based OW-CPA scheme into a deterministic variant with rigorous security proof; (3) we generalize the SPAKE framework to support our construction, achieving minimal-assumption post-quantum AKE. Our implementation benchmarks demonstrate state-of-the-art efficiency, showing that relaxing security from IND-CCA to OW-CCA—while preserving adaptive security—strikes a practical balance between robustness and performance, making it viable for deployment in constrained environments like IoT and connected vehicles.

item.title: Midpoint Reset: A Full-Round Poseidon Collision from an Adaptively Chosen MDS Matrix
item.description:
## Key Contribution This paper presents the first explicit full-round (28 rounds) compression collision for the KoalaBear Poseidon instance with parameters $(t,\alpha,R_F,R_P)=(16,3,8,20)$, under an adaptive-chosen-MDS-matrix setting where round constants are fixed before the linear layer.
## Method & Result The attack constructs a single linear layer that simultaneously controls two execution paths by tracking their midpoint and half-difference. In each two-round block, a prescribed image cancels the midpoint against the next round constant, resetting it to zero, while two reused images confine the half-difference to a one-dimensional subspace. A scalar recurrence closes the final difference under feed-forward.
The resulting MDS matrix satisfies all prescribed checks and yields a collision across all 16 output coordinates. The construction reduces to low-degree equations and admits a parameter family, proving the collision is not an isolated case.
## Significance This work exposes an adaptive correlation between fixed round constants and a subsequently chosen linear layer that matrix-only verification cannot detect, highlighting a new security gap in Poseidon-style hash designs.

item.title: Revisiting the Transferability of Chosen- to Known-plaintext Attacks and Applications to Round-reduced AES
item.description:
## Core Contribution This paper revisits differential-based cryptanalysis under the **random known-plaintext (RKP) model**, where attackers cannot choose inputs. Focusing on AES, we derive the **best-known distinguishers and attacks** for all versions, improving prior RKP results by **at least one round**. Notably, we show that Demirci-Selcuk meet-in-the-middle attacks with differential enumeration remain effective in this setting without approaching the full codebook.
## Key Findings We demonstrate that optimal differential trails under chosen-plaintext models are **not necessarily optimal** in the RKP model, and better trails can replace them. While our attacks do not threaten full AES security, this work is the **first systematic study** of advanced differential attacks in the RKP model, encouraging cryptographers to consider this practical attack scenario in future research.

item.title: $\textsf{Sluice}$: Prove-Phase Bounded-Memory Groth16 via Read-Write Streaming
item.description:
## Core Contribution We present **Sluice**, a read-write streaming Groth16 prover that reduces prove-phase random-access memory from $\mathcal{O}(N)$ to $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ once CRS, QAP, and witness are materialized as private streams. The standard Groth16 interface is preserved: 3-element proofs, 3-pairing verification, and unchanged verifier contracts.
## Key Technique The main innovation is **Split-Butterfly-Merge (SBM)**, an NTT algorithm in the read-write streaming model achieving $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ memory, $\mathcal{O}(N \log N)$ total I/O, and $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ sequential passes over external storage. Combined with streaming sparse R1CS evaluation and chunked Pippenger MSM, this yields a verifier-compatible proving path that trades RAM for sequential I/O and wall-clock time.
## Results Implemented over BN-254, Sluice produces valid 128-byte proofs up to $N=2^{25}$. At $N=2^{23}$, Sluice succeeds under an 8GB Linux cgroup cap, while the standard prover is killed under 8GB and 12GB caps, succeeding only at 16GB. These results position Sluice as a storage-rich, RAM-limited proving option rather than a replacement for optimized in-memory provers.

item.title: Enabling Threshold Custody for the Lightning Network with Nested Threshold Multi-Signatures
item.description:
## Core Contribution This paper introduces **Iceberg**, the first practical construction for nested threshold MuSig2 signatures, enabling unilateral threshold custody deployment on today's Lightning Network without modifying Bitcoin, the Lightning protocol, or channel counterparties. The key innovation is formalizing *nested threshold multi-signatures*—a new primitive that thresholdizes one participant inside an established two-party MuSig2 protocol while preserving its nonce exchange and message flow.
## Results & Impact We prove Iceberg's security, integrate a prototype into a production Lightning node, and benchmark its performance. Measurements show that thresholdized channels sustain over **93% payment throughput** of unmodified endpoints when tolerating one corrupted member. This work eliminates the single-key vulnerability of channel endpoints, making threshold custody practically deployable for the first time in Lightning Network—a system securing hundreds of millions of dollars—with only modest overhead.

item.title: Fully Homomorphic Encryption with Chosen-Ciphertext Security from LWE
item.description:
## Abstract This paper constructs the first (1-hop) fully homomorphic encryption (FHE) scheme with **chosen-ciphertext (CCA) security** under the **learning with errors (LWE)** assumption in the standard model. Security relies solely on **circular-secure LWE**, matching the assumption required for CPA-secure FHE. The scheme achieves a notion **strictly stronger than CCA1**, whereas all prior CCA1-secure FHE schemes required either the random oracle model or non-falsifiable assumptions.
The construction follows the **Naor-Yung double encryption paradigm**, but replaces the general ZK-SNARKs used in previous works with a **specialized succinct argument** for proving FHE ciphertext validity. This argument is built from **batch arguments for NP** and a new primitive called **predicate extractable commitment**, which may be of independent interest. This novel approach avoids strong assumptions while maintaining CCA security, representing a significant theoretical advance in standard-model FHE.

item.title: G-CARL: Grounded Checklist-Aligned Reward Learning for Patient-Oriented Medical Report Interpretation
item.description: ## Overview We introduce **PMRI (Patient-oriented Medical Report Interpretation)**, a novel open-ended multimodal generation task requiring models to explain medical reports accurately and accessibly based on user queries and dialogue history. To address the coupled yet distinct objectives of evidence-grounded factuality and patient-friendly communication, we propose **G-CARL**, a grounded checklist-aligned reinforcement learning framework. It combines multi-source retrieval for atomic claim verification with context-aware, instance-specific weighted checklists, providing structured supervision without constraining response diversity. We also build **MMedReport**, a real-world benchmark with a clinician-designed three-dimensional evaluation protocol. Extensive experiments show G-CARL consistently outperforms existing post-training baselines in overall quality, claim-level precision, and checklist recall, with clinician pairwise preference confirming its superior accuracy and alignment with patient needs.

item.title: An Agentic Approach for Active Data Collection, Travel Behavior Modeling, and Weather-Sensitive Demand Prediction
item.description:
## Core Contribution This study introduces a **three-agent workflow** that unifies conversational data collection, structured processing, and behavior prediction—addressing the traditional disconnect between survey design and modeling in travel behavior research.
## Methods & Results A chatbot-administered, image-augmented stated-preference survey captured mode choices from student commuters under five weather scenarios (454 observations). Nine local LLMs (2B–35B parameters) were benchmarked against multinomial logit, logistic regression, and random forest. The best text-only zero-shot LLM achieved **69.9%** five-class accuracy (matching random forest at 69.6%), while the top vision-based configuration reached **71.5%** using identical weather images shown to respondents. Habitual travel information yielded the most consistent gains; expert framing outperformed role-play; and few-shot prompting improved several models with rapid saturation.
## Significance This work demonstrates the first auditable, multi-agent coordination of conversational surveys, conventional econometric models, machine learning, and multimodal LLM prediction—offering a replicable framework for weather-sensitive demand forecasting and broader behavioral research.

item.title: AI4AI-Bench: Benchmarking LLM Agents in Algorithmic Design for Recursive Self-Improvement
item.description:
## Core Contribution We introduce **AI4AI-Bench**, the first benchmark isolating whether LLM agents can design training algorithms—the key capability for recursive self-improvement. It comprises 10 frozen research repositories spanning diverse training algorithm families. Each agent gets 4 hours on one B300 GPU to rewrite a training algorithm; the rewritten code is then rerun from scratch for up to 12 hours and scored against the original algorithm under identical conditions. All metrics are mapped to a common scale (0 = uninformative model, 0.1 = repository baseline, 1.0 = task optimum).
## Key Results Across 29 configurations of 6 systems on all 10 tasks, the mean score is **0.166**, with the best system reaching 0.250—closing less than one-fifth of the gap between existing algorithms and optimal performance. Notably, most submissions never alter how the model learns; the minority that do average 0.226 versus 0.126 for the rest. Increased reasoning effort primarily encourages agents to attempt learning-algorithm changes, raising such submissions from 8% to 64% and mean scores from 0.094 to 0.196.
## Availability We release the full task suite, evaluators, and all scored submissions to enable reproducible measurement as these systems evolve.

item.title: Pandora's AI Model Routing Box: Efficient Allocation with Costly Value Estimation
item.description:
## Core Contribution
This paper formalizes model routing in heterogeneous AI systems as a **Pandora's Box problem**—optimal search with costly inspection—where estimating each specialist's value incurs a cost. Under a Gaussian signal model, we derive closed-form value-of-information expressions that determine when refining estimation is worthwhile.
## Methods & Results
We propose **Pandora's Router** (centralized) and **Pandora's Bidder** (decentralized). Experiments across three domains (multi-LLM benchmarks, retrieval-augmented specialists, variable-reasoning LLMs) show the Router matches exhaustive-estimation routing quality while querying expensive estimators far less often. In decentralized settings, value-of-information reasoning improves allocative efficiency when competing estimates are accurate, but may increase strategic specialists' utility at others' expense under noisy estimates.
## Key Takeaway
This work bridges classical search theory with modern AI routing, offering a principled cost-quality tradeoff framework and opening new directions for distributed expert collaboration.

item.title: MidTool: Mid-training Data Synthesis for Agentic Tool Use
item.description:
## Core Contribution This paper introduces **MidTool**, an open corpus construction pipeline for mid-training LLMs on general tool use—a capability less explored than reasoning or coding in this training stage. The pipeline synthesizes supervision from real-world tool APIs, MCP skills, and document-grounded workflows, combined with large-scale web, PDF, and code data.
## Key Findings Mid-training Qwen3-4B/8B-Base on MidTool-Mix consistently improves downstream performance across **BFCL, tau2-Bench, and MCP Universe** under both SFT and RL, outperforming baselines. The design targets four core skills: recognizing tool affordances, grounding arguments, composing tool workflows, and recovering from incomplete information.
## Conclusion General tool use, like other critical LLM capabilities, benefits significantly from dedicated mid-training rather than being left entirely to post-training—offering a reproducible recipe for building stronger tool-using agents.

item.title: Inject, Align, Recover: Staged Post-Training for Retrieval-Free Document Knowledge Internalization
item.description: We study **document knowledge internalization**—converting a fixed corpus into parametric knowledge for retrieval-free question answering. We propose **IAR (Inject, Align, Recover)**, a three-stage post-training framework that separates structured knowledge injection (via continuation, rewrite, and instruction-conditioned reconstruction), QA behavior alignment (answer-only supervision), and general ability recovery (via model merging with the base instruction model). Across Common Corpus and CCI datasets, and across Llama, Phi, Qwen, and SmolLM families, IAR improves the domain-general frontier. In the main comparison, IAR outperforms Vanilla SFT on all four metrics in 7 of 8 dataset-model settings, with average gains of **3.6 points** in domain QA accuracy and **12.1 points** in mean general performance (IFEval, MMLU, MSBench). Extended baselines show LoRA and FAPM can win individual general metrics, but among methods achieving leading domain internalization, IAR retains one of the strongest general profiles. This staged design offers a new paradigm for balancing domain specialization and general capability retention.

item.title: Break It Down, Pass It On: Cross-Task Skill Transfer in LLM Agents
item.description: This paper systematically investigates how skill induction methods affect cross-task transfer reliability in LLM agents. Through controlled experiments, the authors compare two dimensions: induction granularity (task-level vs. subtask-level) and skill format (text vs. code). Key findings show that task-level skills often degrade performance below the no-memory baseline, while subtask-level skills improve it on average, and text skills transfer better than code skills. To explain these results, they propose two complementary properties—specificity (how closely a skill matches real tasks) and abstractness (how evenly relevance distributes across tasks)—which individually fail to predict success but jointly form a **skill utility score**. This score, computable from skills and task descriptions alone without task execution, consistently correlates with transfer success and serves as a practical pre-run diagnostic for skill memories. The work provides crucial insights for designing reliable experience accumulation mechanisms in LLM agents.

item.title: Catching the Rug: Early Prediction of Fraudulent Memecoins on Solana via Machine Learning
item.description:
## Core Contribution This paper pioneers early detection of fraudulent memecoins (rug pulls) on the Solana blockchain, using a dataset of 6.4 million tokens over 7 months. Unlike Ethereum-based attacks exploiting smart contract backdoors, Solana rug pulls are driven by liquidity manipulation and social dynamics, requiring a different detection paradigm.
## Method & Key Results Using only the first 5 minutes of trading data, we show that classic machine learning, especially XGBoost, achieves robust performance in identifying potential rug pulls, despite the absence of code-level features. Cross-platform experiments between PumpFun and Raydium reveal that multi-source data fusion significantly mitigates domain shift, enhancing detection reliability.
## Impact This work provides the first practical framework for real-time investor protection on high-throughput blockchains, demonstrating that short-horizon prediction is both feasible and effective. The findings advance understanding of DeFi fraud and offer a scalable solution for emerging token ecosystems.

item.title: Learning When to Think: Adaptive Reasoning for Test-Time Compute Allocation
item.description:
## Core Contribution This paper introduces an **adaptive reasoning allocation mechanism** for language models, enabling them to choose their reasoning effort per problem via a first-token router that selects among three modes: *NoThink*, *Short*, or *Long*.
## Method & Key Results The choice is learned end-to-end via **GRPO** without a separate router, using shaped rewards and hard token caps to keep modes distinct. On a 1.5B distilled model trained on MATH: - The three modes emerge without collapse, with shorter modes proving more accurate than *Long*—confirming difficulty-based routing. - Averaged over three seeds, accuracy on MATH500 stays close to baseline (0.782 vs. 0.796) while **response length drops 41%** (from 4,796 to 2,811 tokens). - The policy **transfers zero-shot** to other benchmarks, achieving 76% token reduction on GSM8K with higher accuracy at similar length.
## Significance This work demonstrates that models can **autonomously decide how much to reason**, offering a practical path to efficient test-time compute allocation while preserving accuracy—a key step toward cost-effective reasoning systems.

item.title: QUASAR: A Quantum-Classical Neural Network for SAR Satellite Physical-Layer Authentication
item.description:
## Core Contribution We present **QUASAR**, the first quantum-classical hybrid architecture for physical-layer authentication (PLA) of X-band SAR satellites, combining a CNN spectrogram encoder with a variational quantum circuit (VQC). Unlike prior PLA limited to sub-6 GHz and classical deep learning, QUASAR captures IQ phase nonlinearities distinctive to satellite hardware.
## Key Results - **Data efficiency**: Matches classical baselines using only **10% of training data**; - **Superior accuracy** at equal data budgets; - **Adversarial robustness**: Rejects spoofing in **89.7%** (replay), **94.1%** (crafted-IQ injection), and **81.3%** (space-borne spoofing) of attempts.
## Significance QUASAR establishes the first quantum-enhanced physical-layer classifier for satellite constellations, opening a novel research avenue for secure satellite communications.

item.title: Prompt-Conditioned Channel Attention for Hierarchical Feature Modulation toward Anatomy-Agnostic Segmentation
item.description: **We introduce Prompt-Conditioned Channel Attention (PCCA)**, a novel modulation mechanism enabling deep, hierarchical integration of semantic prompts in encoder-decoder networks. PCCA extracts compact channel descriptors via pooling, projects them into a shared space, and fuses them through a gated excitation mechanism to produce prompt-aware attention weights, which adaptively recalibrate features across multiple stages. **Built on PCCA, PROMISE-Net** (with CNN and Transformer variants) was evaluated on four benchmarks: ISIC-Lesion, Kvasir-Polyp, CAMUS-Cardiac, and Kvasir-Instrument. **PROMISE-CNN achieved relative IoU gains of 10.4%, 8.7%, 0.8%, and 3.4%** over U-Net, while **PROMISE-Txformer achieved 7.6%, 23.0%, 2.1%, and 1.1%** over UNETR, respectively. These consistent improvements across architectures, modalities, and anatomical targets establish PCCA as a scalable, generalizable framework for prompt-aware medical image segmentation.

item.title: Electronic Navigational Chart Change Classification
item.description:
## Core Contribution This paper presents an automated classification method for Electronic Navigational Chart (ENC) changes, addressing the labor-intensive manual review bottleneck in hydrographic offices. We propose a baseline encoding scheme that converts complex vector data changes into structured tabular format, featuring a **spatial context encoder** (enriching representations with surrounding geographic features) and an **attribute encoder** (capturing nuanced object property descriptions).
## Key Results Evaluated on two operational datasets comprising 1,308 chart pairs with over 100,000 modifications, tuned gradient-boosted trees achieved **90% and 94% accuracy** respectively—a 5–7% improvement over default models without spatial context and attribute embeddings.
## Significance The findings demonstrate the viability of integrating machine learning into operational geospatial pipelines for ENC maintenance, enhancing maritime safety. The success of simple spatial aggregation methods also provides a foundation for evaluating advanced spatial representation learning techniques in future work.

item.title: Daedalus-150M: A Convolution-Attention Hybrid Designed for CPU Inference
item.description:
## Design & Results **Daedalus-150M** is a convolution-attention hybrid CPU-first language model. Only 6 of 18 blocks retain full attention; the other 12 use short convolutions with fixed two-timestep memory, so two-thirds of the network never re-reads a growing cache. Trained from scratch on 59.9B tokens, it scores **47.31** on a five-task benchmark (pre-set bar: 42.20), surpassing GPT-2 124M, Pythia-160M, OPT-125M, and GPT-neo-125M (trained on 3–6× more data), and exceeding MobileLLM-125M's published score despite that model seeing 1T tokens. Validation bits-per-byte is 0.8685.
In a controlled comparison against an all-attention model of equal size and data, the hybrid wins the chosen quality metric by 0.81%, matches downstream tasks, yields a 6.3% smaller 4-bit file, and decodes 1.76× faster at 2048-token context (2.08× vs. an external similar-size model). Speed advantage is near zero at empty context and grows with length—matching the mechanism's prediction, not just a leaner model. A simple bandwidth estimate predicts only 1.17×, so memory volume alone doesn't explain the gap. Failed attempts include unmitigated 4-bit quality loss, ~half inert convolution channels, and an oversized vocabulary.

item.title: ContractScrub: A benchmark for final review of legal contracts
item.description:
## Core Contribution We introduce **ContractScrub**, the first benchmark for evaluating LLMs on contract scrubbing—the final review of legal agreements for errors and inconsistencies. The benchmark comprises contracts hand-crafted by experienced lawyers, covering diverse error categories such as misuse of defined terms, incorrect references, and inconsistent language.
## Key Results Frontier models perform surprisingly poorly: only one model reached 0.75 macro average recall, despite strong performance on seemingly related general benchmarks (e.g., long-context reasoning, NER). This reveals a critical gap between general capabilities and domain-specific expertise.
## Significance ContractScrub highlights the practical limits of current models and underscores the necessity of narrowly targeted, domain-specific benchmarks for measuring real-world impact in legal AI. It provides a standardized tool for future model development and legal technology evaluation.

item.title: MemTrapBench: Benchmarking Cognitive Traps in LLM Memory Use
item.description:
## Core Contribution We introduce **MemTrapBench**, the first benchmark systematically evaluating *cognitive traps* in LLM memory use—cases where faithfully recorded, semantically relevant memories distort reasoning or beliefs and degrade current-task performance.
## Key Findings Across two model families and five memory frameworks, **all existing memory strategies underperform the no-memory baseline**, with the strongest method dropping over 10% in performance. This reveals a critical blind spot in prior memory evaluation.
## Proposed Method We propose **AdaptiveMem**, a lightweight inference-time method that instructs LLMs to actively avoid memory traps. It mitigates cognitive traps on MemTrapBench while preserving or improving performance on standard memory benchmarks, demonstrating effectiveness across diverse memory frameworks.
## Impact Our work highlights that memory quality must be measured not only by retrieval accuracy but also by its *influence on reasoning*, offering a new evaluation paradigm and a practical mitigation strategy for robust memory-augmented LLMs.

item.title: The Third Restructuring of Software Form: From the Three-Tier Architecture to Storage, Models, and Agents
item.description:
## Core Contribution This paper identifies a third paradigm shift in software form—**Software 3.0**—where context and reasoning, rather than instructions or data, determine behavior. The terminal architecture converges to three components: a generalized database (unified persistent state), a large model (reasoning core), and an agent (execution loop).
## Key Argument In the traditional three-tier architecture, the UI layer is absorbed by on-demand interface generation; the business-logic layer is repartitioned by "expressibility × criticality" into model reasoning and storage constraints, with residual deterministic logic as tools; only the data layer survives as permanent infrastructure.
## Evidence & Boundaries The authors formalize this convergence thesis, present a reference architecture, and validate it with prototypes and a live model. They systematically delineate the thesis's applicability domain, bounded by determinism, cost, security, and verifiability. The thesis holds for tasks that are expressible, verifiable, externally stateful, and tool-complete—reshaping developer roles, the database industry, and software engineering practice.

item.title: From Agent Behaviour to Agent-Friendly Documentation: An Empirical Study of How Coding Agents Discover, Read, and Write Technical Documentation
item.description:
## Overview This behaviour-grounded study investigates how coding agents interact with technical documentation, using two public datasets: 557 agentic sessions (SWE-chat) and 33,097 agentic pull requests (AIDev), yielding 3,033 documentation interactions and 690,260 file-level change records.
## Key Findings Four results challenge current documentation practices. First, agents predominantly consult agent-facing artefacts (instruction files and working notes, 60.5% of interactions), far exceeding classical documentation (10.6%) and API references (1.3%). Second, the consultation–editing link is ambiguous: adjacent transition probability is 0.002 (unadjusted lift 1.05), but a stage-adjusted model yields OR 1.33 [1.09, 1.62]. Third, no documentation-based validation sequence was observed; consultation is negatively associated with immediate testing (adjusted OR 0.39 [0.25, 0.60]). Fourth, consultation is mostly self-initiated (70.2% vs. 7.5% failure-driven), and code precedes documentation 4.7× more often in multi-commit PRs.
## Contribution We propose a **two-lobed cycle** model of agent–documentation interaction, replacing the linear-journey assumption, and show that the presumed properties of "agent-friendly" documentation—actionability and verifiability—lack consistent behavioural support. The full pipeline, coding scheme, and event-level data are released publicly.

item.title: A Standardized Framework for Machine Learning in Power System Protection
item.description:
## Core Contribution This paper proposes a standardization-oriented framework for evaluating machine-learning-based power system protection, defining seven required study dimensions: protection objective, physical scope, observability, timing/decision windows, targets and sample validity, validation protocol, and evaluation outputs.
## Key Results Validated on the PROTECT-90 benchmark (9022 simulated episodes from a 90 kV double-line topology), a multi-layer perceptron achieved a five-fold mean macro-F1 of 0.991 ± 0.001 for fault classification and a localization mean absolute error of 10.20 ± 0.25% of line length under centralized sensing, 20 ms windows, and episode-grouped validation. Extending the decision horizon to 50 ms preserved task-dependent asymmetry; reduced observability doubled localization error but barely affected classification. A synchronized two-ended locator outperformed learning locators under richer clean information, and measurement degradation showed clean performance did not imply robustness.
## Significance The framework converts implicit evaluation assumptions into explicit, reproducible evidence, enabling more comparable, auditable, and certification-oriented assessment of ML protection functions.

item.title: DARS: Dual-Level Credit Assignment RL with Structured Reasoning for Instruction-Based Image Editing
item.description:
**DARS** is a reinforcement learning framework for dual-level credit assignment in instruction-based image editing, which typically follows a planner-renderer pipeline (VLM plans, diffusion executes). Training with only final-image rewards is inefficient because failures do not indicate whether to adjust the planner or renderer, and planner errors are hard to localize in free-form reasoning.
DARS addresses this via: (1) *cross-module* multi-plan multi-render rollouts that estimate reward variability for soft module routing, plus rollout mean rewards for an adaptive curriculum; (2) *intra-planner* four-field structured reasoning that enables prefix-gated rewards and token-level advantage reweighting, converting outcome feedback into localized supervision.
Experiments on five benchmarks show DARS consistently outperforms a Joint RL baseline under identical backbone, data, reward model, and rollout budget, with the largest gains on reasoning-intensive edits. This demonstrates that explicit credit assignment across and within modules substantially improves training efficiency and final editing quality.

item.title: Towards Professional Tennis Styles for Humanoid Robots with Adaptive Motion Planning and Tracking
item.description: **AdaPT** is a hierarchical framework enabling humanoid robots to learn professional tennis serving and rally styles from broadcast videos. The planner generates stylistic motions, while a tracker executes them, but the sim-to-real gap degrades tracking on real hardware—an issue exacerbated by autoregressive planning and perception noise. To bridge this gap, we introduce an adaptation mechanism that trains the tracker on randomized execution speeds and conditions the planner on a learned motion-speed adapter. Experiments on Unitree G1 and the full-size Dobot Atom (1.7m) demonstrate robust in-the-wild serving without motion capture, confirming the mechanism’s effectiveness. The work also provides practical insights for future humanoid ball-sports systems.

item.title: Evidence-Gated Task and Motion Planning with Vision-Language Models
item.description:
## Core Contribution We propose **Evidence Acquisition and Feasibility Gating (EAFG)**, a framework that integrates Vision-Language Models (VLMs) with Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) for long-horizon manipulation under partial observability. EAFG actively acquires visual evidence via VLM-generated exploratory subgoals, then applies a feasibility gate to decide whether to proceed, gather more evidence, or halt.
## Key Results In cooking tasks with ambiguous object usage, EAFG improved recipe completion by discovering task-relevant objects *before* planning. For instructions requiring an absent object, it promoted appropriate halt decisions and reduced repeated failed manipulation attempts.
## Significance By coupling evidence acquisition with gated decision-making, EAFG bridges the gap between VLM prior knowledge and actual environmental state, enhancing both task success rate and operational safety in real-world robotic scenarios.

item.title: SABET-QA: Temporal Knowledge Graph Question Answering
item.description:
## Core Contribution We introduce **SABET-QA**, a novel framework for temporal knowledge graph question answering that addresses the limitation of single-pass embedding methods in multi-step temporal reasoning.
## Key Innovations - **Bidirectional entity-temporal scoring** enables iterative state refinement across hops - **Slot-aware contextualization** aligns question semantics with temporal KG embeddings - **Differentiable working memory** supports progressive hypothesis correction - **Auxiliary temporal boundaries** provide coarse supervision when available
## Results & Impact Experiments on CronQuestions, Complex-CronQuestions, MultiTQ, and TimeQuestions show consistent improvements over strong baselines, with the largest gains on complex multi-step temporal queries. This work establishes a new paradigm for temporal reasoning, moving beyond static embedding matching toward iterative, time-aware inference.

item.title: Let's Scale Step by Step: Compute-Efficient Hyperparameter Transfer for Large-Scale Mixture-of-Experts
item.description: This paper presents a **compute-efficient two-step hyperparameter transfer framework** for large-scale Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models. First, we adapt Maximal Update Parameterization (μP) to MoE architectures with Multi-head Latent Attention and the Muon optimizer, demonstrating consistent learning-rate transfer across model widths. Second, we establish a scaling law along the token dimension, using linear regression on optimal values from small proxy models to extrapolate learning rates to trillion-token horizons with high fidelity (R²=0.95). Applied to pretraining a 155B-total/17B-active foundation model from scratch, the predicted hyperparameters yielded stable training and strong evaluation results, confirming that small-model proxy runs suffice to determine optimal configurations for full-scale MoE training with minimal ablation cost.

item.title: On the Applicability of Safety Nets: A Safety-By-Design Solution for Certifying Neural Networks
item.description: ## Core Contribution This paper presents the **first systematic analysis** of the trade-off between neural network and lookup table sizes in Safety Nets—a Safety-by-Design solution for certifying AI-based aviation systems. By comparing diverse architectures, we identify optimal configurations: **3-5 hidden layers with 50-100 nodes per layer**, combined with one-hot encoding, achieve the best balance. In these settings, neural networks accurately represent **≥97% of data**, while compact lookup tables handle residual errors, reducing system size by **nearly three orders of magnitude**—fitting within current avionics memory budgets while guaranteeing 100% correct outputs across the discretized input space, as mandated by EASA. We also release the **first open-source implementation** for HCAS and VCAS with replicable results, demonstrating a practical pathway toward certifiable AI in aviation. This work establishes Safety Nets as a viable solution for safety-critical applications beyond aviation.

item.title: A three-dimensional typology of agency for advanced AI systems
item.description:
## A Three-Dimensional Typology of Agency for Advanced AI Systems
This paper addresses a critical gap in AI research: the lack of a systematic framework for classifying the *type* of agency instantiated by frontier AI systems, particularly non-moral forms. Drawing on philosophy, ethics, legal theory, and sociology, the authors propose a three-dimensional typology: the **nature** of agency (moral or legal), its **mode** (individual or collective), and its **locus** (human or non-human). Combining these dimensions yields eight possible agency instantiations, categorized as conventional, contested, or controversial.
The key innovation is the deliberate **separation of legal from moral agency**, which creates conceptual space for recognizing individual, legal, non-human agency without presupposing moral status. The authors argue this distinction becomes increasingly vital as instrumental goal-seeking complicates the attribution of AI actions to specific human actors. This framework offers a rigorous analytical tool for governance, liability, and human-AI interaction debates, moving beyond anthropomorphic assumptions while acknowledging AI's operational independence.

item.title: An Inclusive and Lightweight Approach to Federated Continual Learning for Cultural Heritage
item.description:
## Abstract
**Objective:** This paper addresses federated continual learning (FCL) for cultural heritage, where data are distributed across institutions, access-restricted, and continuously evolving.
**Method:** We propose **FedCurv-DR**, a lightweight regularization-based FCL strategy that accumulates parameter-importance estimates across clients and tasks to mitigate catastrophic forgetting, while updating these estimates only at fixed intervals to reduce communication and computation overhead.
**Evaluation:** Using the WikiArt dataset for genre classification with evolving styles, we assess performance, energy consumption, and fairness.
**Key Results:** FedCurv-DR effectively reduces forgetting, maintains competitive accuracy, and achieves a balanced trade-off among performance, fairness, and energy efficiency—offering a sustainable and practical solution for collaborative AI in cultural heritage.

item.title: Contrastive Mixed Prompt Learning for Incomplete Multimodal Sentiment Analysis with Unseen Modality Combination
item.description: This paper tackles **Incomplete Multimodal Sentiment Analysis with Unseen Modality Combinations (IMSAUMC)**, where test-time modality combinations differ from training. We propose **Contrastive Mixed Prompt Learning (CMPL)**, featuring label-guided contrastive feature learning, soft-routed modality-combination prompts, and three prompt contrastive strategies. These components jointly enable robust cross-modal representations and effective generalization to unseen modality combinations. Extensive experiments on three benchmarks show CMPL achieves **>5% accuracy improvement** over state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating strong robustness in diverse missing-pattern scenarios.

item.title: Optimal Skill Selection for LLM Agents with Provable Bicriteria Guarantees
item.description:
## Core Contribution This paper presents the **first principled model** for how selected skill sets affect LLM agent execution outcomes, formulating skill selection as a budget-constrained optimization that maximizes monotone submodular benefit minus context penalty.
## Method & Theory The authors propose **Best Prefix Selection (BPS)**, a polynomial-time algorithm, and prove the **first bicriteria $(1-1/e, 1)$ approximation guarantee** for skill selection, with an optimal benefit coefficient achievable in polynomial time.
## Key Results On a contamination-controlled BigCodeBench variant, BPS achieves **0.73 task success** (vs. 0.20–0.52 for released routers, retrievers, and executor self-selection) while using **28% fewer tokens** than the strongest released router.
## Significance This work bridges the gap between heuristic skill retrieval and provable optimization, offering both theoretical guarantees and superior empirical performance for token-efficient LLM agent design.

item.title: Open-Vocabulary 3D Object Detection with Co-Distillation Discovery and Dual Guidance Robust Training
item.description:
## Core Contribution This paper tackles the **open-vocabulary 3D object detection** challenge, where existing two-stage pipelines suffer from unreliable novel-object discovery (inaccurate localization and mismatched classification). We propose a novel framework with two key innovations:
1. **Co-distillation discovery**: A comprehensive score integrating geometric consistency, structural objectness, and semantic certainty, refined via Hungarian matching to distill high-quality pseudo-labels. 2. **Dual-guidance robust training**: Scene-awareness-guided uncertainty regularization for the regression head, plus LLM-guided hierarchical alignment for the classification head, jointly mitigating noise from imprecise boxes and semantic ambiguity.
Experiments on SUN RGB-D and ScanNetV2 demonstrate consistent and significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods. Our code is publicly available, facilitating reproducibility and future research.

item.title: Rethinking Patch Based Multivariate Time Series Forecasting with Semantic Structured Partitioning
item.description:
## Core Contribution We propose **SCPaT**, a Transformer-based framework for multivariate time series forecasting (MTSF) that introduces **semantic structured partitioning** to overcome the limitations of existing patch-based methods (fixed, multi-scale, and extendable partitioning).
## Key Innovations SCPaT operates in three stages: (1) **adaptive semantic unit generation** to segment sequences into semantically consistent units; (2) **dynamic semantic graph construction** to model directed dependencies among units and organize them into higher-order semantic blocks; (3) an **importance-aware routing mechanism** that dispatches different semantic blocks to specialized experts for customized modeling.
## Results Extensive experiments on **12 real-world datasets** demonstrate that SCPaT consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, validating its effectiveness in capturing heterogeneous temporal patterns and inter-pattern interactions. This work provides a new perspective on patch-based forecasting by emphasizing semantic structure over fixed granularity.

item.title: Designing Human-mediated AI Guidance: Ready Together for Personalized Family Emergency Preparedness
item.description: This paper introduces a **human-mediated AI guidance framework**, addressing scenarios where AI-generated content requires human interpretation before reaching end users—particularly when recipients are less experienced or vulnerable. The framework is explored through **Ready Together**, an AI-supported family emergency preparedness system where parents mediate personalized AI content for their children via interactive, family-centered activities. Using qualitative, design-oriented methods (semi-structured interviews and co-design), the authors identified key challenges in family preparedness, including difficulties discussing emergencies with children and preferences for interactive learning. An interactive prototype was subsequently evaluated through pilot and heuristic evaluations, yielding positive responses to personalized recommendations and practical activities. Preliminary findings suggest that human-mediated AI guidance can support context-sensitive family preparedness while preserving parents' interpretive responsibility, offering a novel design paradigm for human-AI collaboration in sensitive domains.

item.title: Towards Quantifying Benchmark Optimization in ASR Models
item.description: This paper introduces a methodology to quantify benchmark optimization in Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) models, targeting scenarios where audio underdetermines the reference transcript. Using three behavioral probes—reference disagreement, masked-number recovery, and orthographic switching—we reveal that top-scoring open-source models output verbatim benchmark reference spans even when audio is contradictory, masked, or ambiguous. Mechanistic probes show these models rely on narrow acoustic cues to override faithful audio transcription in favor of a benchmark-optimized policy. Crucially, this behavior can be causally manipulated via low-rank linear steering or audio appending, demonstrating that high benchmark scores may inflate perceived performance without reflecting genuine general-purpose transcription ability. Our work provides a framework for detecting such artifacts and calls for more robust evaluation protocols.
